title: MATH2010 Module 07: Vector Spaces and Subspaces & Linearly Independent Sets

questions.q: Let W = {(x, y) : x² + y² ≤ 1} (the closed unit disk). Is W a subspace of ℝ²?
choices: Yes, because the zero vector is in W.
No: (1, 0) is in W, but 2·(1, 0) = (2, 0) is not, so W is not closed under scalar multiplication.
No: the zero vector is not in W.
Yes, because W is closed under addition.
questions.explain: 0² + 0² = 0 ≤ 1, so the zero vector IS in W. That test passes, so it settles nothing. Scalar multiplication fails: (1, 0) is in W, but (2, 0) gives 4 > 1. Addition fails too: (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) gives 2 > 1. One specific counterexample is enough to answer 'no'.

questions.q: If a subset H of a vector space V contains the zero vector of V, then H is a subspace of V.
questions.explain: Containing 0 is necessary but not sufficient. The unit disk x² + y² ≤ 1 contains 0 but is not closed under scalar multiplication. H must also be closed under addition and under scalar multiplication.

questions.q: Which of these sets is a subspace of ℝ²?
questions.explain: x + 2y = 0 is a homogeneous linear equation. Its solution set is span{(−2, 1)} = Nul[1 2], a line through the origin. x + 2y = 1 fails the zero test (0 ≠ 1). xy ≥ 0 is not closed under addition: (2, 1) + (−1, −2) = (1, −1) has xy = −1. y = x² is not closed under scaling: (1, 1) is in it, but 2(1, 1) = (2, 2) has 2 ≠ 4.

questions.q: Which of these sets are subspaces of ℙ₄ (polynomials of degree at most 4)?
choices: All polynomials at² − bt, where a, b ∈ ℝ
All polynomials t² + at + 7, where a ∈ ℝ
All p in ℙ₄ with p(0) = 0
All p in ℙ₄ with p(0) = 1
All polynomials a + bt³, where a, b ∈ ℝ
questions.explain: at² − bt = span{t², t} and a + bt³ = span{1, t³}, and every span is a subspace. For p(0) = 0: the zero polynomial has value 0 at 0, (p + q)(0) = 0 + 0 = 0, and (cp)(0) = c·0 = 0. t² + at + 7 does not contain the zero polynomial, because its t²-coefficient is fixed at 1 and its constant term at 7. p(0) = 1 fails because the zero polynomial has p(0) = 0 ≠ 1.

questions.q: Why is S = {t² + at + 7 : a ∈ ℝ} NOT a subspace of ℙ₇?
choices: Its polynomials have degree 2, and ℙ₇ contains only polynomials of degree exactly 7.
The zero polynomial is not in S: every member has t²-coefficient 1 and constant term 7.
S is closed under addition but fails scalar multiplication only when a is negative.
S is actually a subspace of ℙ₇.
questions.explain: The zero polynomial 0t² + 0t + 0 would need t²-coefficient 0 and constant term 0, so it is not in S. Closure fails too: (t² + 7) + (t² + 7) = 2t² + 14 has t²-coefficient 2. ℙ₇ means degree AT MOST 7, so lower-degree polynomials are allowed in it.

questions.q: ℝ² is a subspace of ℝ³.
questions.explain: Vectors in ℝ² have 2 entries and vectors in ℝ³ have 3, so ℝ² is not even a subset of ℝ³. The plane {(x, y, 0)} is a subspace of ℝ³ that looks like ℝ², but it is not ℝ².

questions.q: Which of these subsets of M₂ₓ₂ (all 2×2 real matrices) are subspaces of M₂ₓ₂?
questions.explain: Diagonal matrices: the zero matrix is diagonal, and sums and scalar multiples keep zeros off the diagonal (0 + 0 = 0, c·0 = 0). Upper triangular works the same way for the entry below the diagonal. Invertible matrices fail because the zero matrix is not invertible (also I + (−I) = 0). The (1,1) = 1 set fails because the zero matrix has (1,1) entry 0.

questions.q: To prove that a set H is a subspace, it is enough to check closure under addition and scalar multiplication for a few specific numerical vectors in H.
questions.explain: A 'yes' needs a general argument with arbitrary u, v in H and an arbitrary scalar c, or writing H as a span. Only a 'no' can be settled by one specific numerical counterexample.

questions.q: Which list gives exactly the subspaces of ℝ³?
choices: {0}, lines through the origin, planes through the origin, and ℝ³
All lines and all planes in ℝ³, together with ℝ³
Lines through the origin, ℝ², and ℝ³
questions.explain: A subspace must contain 0, so lines and planes that miss the origin are out. {0} and the whole space are always subspaces. ℝ² is not a subset of ℝ³.

questions.q: Let H be the set of all vectors of the form (5t, −7t, t), t ∈ ℝ. Which vector v satisfies H = span{v}?
questions.explain: Pull out the parameter: (5t, −7t, t) = t(5, −7, 1). So H = span{(5, −7, 1)}, a line through the origin, and it is a subspace of ℝ³. Any nonzero multiple, such as (10, −14, 2), would also work.

questions.q: Let W = {(x, y) : x + 2y = 0}. Which vector v satisfies W = span{v}?
questions.explain: Solve for x = −2y, so (x, y) = (−2y, y) = y(−2, 1). Check: −2 + 2(1) = 0. (1, 2) holds the coefficients of the equation; it is perpendicular to the line and not on it (1 + 4 = 5 ≠ 0).

questions.q: The set H = {at² − bt : a, b ∈ ℝ} in ℙ₄ is equal to which span?
questions.explain: at² − bt = a·t² + (−b)·t. As b ranges over ℝ, so does −b, so H is all combinations of t² and t. span{t² − t} only gives the multiples c(t² − t), which forces the two coefficients to be tied together.

questions.q: If v₁, …, vₚ are vectors in a vector space V, then span{v₁, …, vₚ} is a subspace of V.
questions.explain: This is the span theorem. It is often the fastest way to show a set is a subspace: write the set as all linear combinations of some fixed vectors.

The third vector repeats the first, so the span is span{(1, −1, −2), (0, −1, 3)}. These two are not multiples, so the span is a plane. Row reducing [v₁ v₂ | b] leaves the bottom row 0 0 | 5b₁ + 3b₂ + b₃, so the span is 5x + 3y + z = 0. Check: 5 − 3 − 2 = 0 and 0 − 3 + 3 = 0.

(1, 1, −2) + (1, −1, 2) = (2, 0, 0), so the third vector is redundant and the span is a plane. Row reducing [A | b] leaves the bottom row 0 0 0 | 2b₂ + b₃, so the span is 2y + z = 0. Check: 2 − 2 = 0, −2 + 2 = 0, 0 + 0 = 0.

questions.q: span{(1, −1, −1), (2, 1, 3)} is a plane through the origin with equation 2x + 5y + cz = 0. Find c.
questions.explain: Each spanning vector must satisfy the equation. (1, −1, −1): 2 − 5 − c = 0 gives c = −3. Check with (2, 1, 3): 4 + 5 − 9 = 0. Row reducing [v₁ v₂ | b] gives −2b₁ − 5b₂ + 3b₃ = 0, the same plane.

questions.q: Which vectors are in span{(1, −1, −1), (2, 1, 3)}?
Is {(1, −1, −2), (0, −1, 3), (1, −1, −2)} linearly independent?
choices: Yes, because none of the vectors is the zero vector.
No, because 1·v₁ + 0·v₂ − 1·v₃ = 0 is a nontrivial dependence relation.
Yes, because v₁ and v₂ are not scalar multiples of each other.
No, because any 3 vectors in ℝ³ are dependent.
questions.explain: v₃ = v₁, so v₁ − v₃ = 0 with weights that are not all zero. Row reduction agrees: only 2 pivots and a free variable in column 3. Three vectors in ℝ³ CAN be independent (for example the standard basis), so that last reason is wrong.

questions.q: Which conditions guarantee that a set of vectors in ℝⁿ is linearly dependent?
choices: The set contains the zero vector.
The set has more than n vectors.
One of the vectors is a linear combination of the others.
The set has fewer than n vectors.
No two of the vectors are scalar multiples of each other.
The same vector appears twice in the set.
questions.explain: 1·0 = 0 is a nontrivial relation. More columns than rows forces a free variable. A vector that is a combination of the others gives a dependence relation. A repeated vector gives 1v − 1v = 0. Having fewer than n vectors says nothing about independence. 'No two are multiples' is not enough once there are 3 or more vectors: (1, 1, −2), (1, −1, 2), (2, 0, 0) are pairwise non-parallel but dependent.

questions.q: Let v₁ = (1, 1, −2), v₂ = (1, −1, 2), v₃ = (2, 0, 0). Find the scalar c such that v₁ + v₂ + c·v₃ = 0.
questions.explain: v₁ + v₂ = (2, 0, 0) = v₃, so v₁ + v₂ − v₃ = 0 and c = −1. This nontrivial relation shows the set is linearly dependent. It matches the null vector (−1, −1, 1) of A = [v₁ v₂ v₃], scaled by −1.

questions.q: A set of two vectors {v₁, v₂} is linearly dependent if and only if one of the vectors is a scalar multiple of the other.
questions.explain: If c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ = 0 with c₁ ≠ 0, then v₁ = (−c₂/c₁)v₂, and the case c₂ ≠ 0 works the same way. Conversely, v₁ = kv₂ gives v₁ − kv₂ = 0. This includes the case where one vector is 0 = 0·(other).

questions.q: Let A = [v₁ ⋯ vₚ]. After row reducing A, the columns v₁, …, vₚ are linearly independent exactly when:
choices: there is a pivot in every row
there is a pivot in every column
Ax = b is consistent for at least one b
questions.explain: Independent means Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution, so there are no free variables and every column has a pivot. A pivot in every row is the test for spanning ℝᵐ. Ax = b is always consistent for b = 0, so the last choice tells you nothing.

questions.q: The set {(1, −1, −1), (2, 1, 3)} is linearly independent.
questions.explain: Two vectors are dependent only if one is a multiple of the other. Here the first entries need a factor of 2 but the second entries need −1, so they are not multiples. Row reduction gives a pivot in both columns.

questions.q: Any set of 4 vectors in ℝ³ is linearly dependent.
questions.explain: A 3×4 matrix has at most 3 pivots, so at least one column has no pivot. That free variable gives a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0.

choices: Yes, because it is linearly independent.
No. It is linearly independent, but two vectors cannot span ℝ³.
No, because it is linearly dependent.
Yes, because it spans a plane through the origin.
questions.explain: A 3×2 matrix has at most 2 pivots, so some row has no pivot and the set does not span ℝ³. It is independent (not multiples), so it is a basis for the plane 2x + 5y − 3z = 0, just not for ℝ³. A basis needs BOTH independence and spanning.

questions.q: If three vectors in ℝ³ are linearly dependent, they cannot span ℝ³.
questions.explain: A = [v₁ v₂ v₃] is square. Dependent means fewer than 3 pivots, so some row has no pivot and the columns do not span. For a square matrix, 'independent', 'spans', and 'invertible' are all equivalent (Invertible Matrix Theorem).

questions.q: Let S = {v₁, v₂, v₃} with v₃ = v₁ + v₂, and let H = span S. Which statement is true?
choices: span{v₁, v₂} is strictly smaller than H
S is a basis for H
questions.explain: Spanning Set Theorem: removing a vector that is a linear combination of the others does not change the span. S is dependent, so it is not a basis. If v₁ and v₂ are independent, then {v₁, v₂} is a basis for H.

questions.q: Which of these sets are bases for ℝ³?
questions.explain: The first set gives a matrix with determinant 1(1 − 0) − 0 + 1(2 − 0) = 3 ≠ 0, so it is a basis. The standard basis is a basis. The second set is dependent (v₁ + v₂ = v₃). Two vectors cannot span ℝ³. Four vectors in ℝ³ are dependent, even though this set does span ℝ³.

questions.q: A basis is a spanning set that is as large as possible.
questions.explain: A basis is a spanning set that is as SMALL as possible, which means it has no redundant vectors. Equivalently, it is an independent set that is as large as possible.

questions.q: Which set is the standard basis for ℙ₂?
questions.explain: Every polynomial a₀ + a₁t + a₂t² in ℙ₂ is a unique combination of 1, t, and t². {t, t²} misses constants, t³ is not in ℙ₂, and one polynomial cannot span ℙ₂.

questions.q: Let v₁, …, vₙ be n vectors in ℝⁿ and A = [v₁ ⋯ vₙ]. Three of these statements are equivalent to {v₁, …, vₙ} being a basis for ℝⁿ. Which one is NOT?
choices: The columns of A span ℝⁿ
questions.explain: A nontrivial solution of Ax = 0 means the columns are dependent, which is the opposite of a basis. For a square matrix, det A ≠ 0, n pivots, columns spanning, and columns independent all go together.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 3, 4), (2, 1, 3), (1, 2, 5). Its reduced echelon form is I₃. What is a basis for Nul A?
questions.explain: There are no free variables, so Ax = 0 has only x = 0 and Nul A = {0}. Its basis is the empty set. {0} is not a basis because any set containing 0 is dependent. Here det A = −10 ≠ 0, so Col A = ℝ³ and the three columns of A form a basis for Col A.

questions.q: Let A be an m×n matrix. Nul A is a subspace of ____, and Col A is a subspace of ____.
questions.explain: For Ax to make sense, x needs n entries (one per column), so Nul A ⊆ ℝⁿ. The columns of A have m entries (one per row), so Col A ⊆ ℝᵐ.

questions.q: A is a 5×7 matrix with 4 pivot columns. How many vectors are in a basis for Nul A?
questions.explain: Pivots + free variables = number of columns, so 7 − 4 = 3 free variables, one basis vector each. A basis for Col A has 4 vectors (the pivot columns), and Col A ≠ ℝ⁵ because that would need a pivot in all 5 rows.

questions.q: The pivot columns of an echelon form of A form a basis for Col A.
questions.explain: Use the pivot columns of the ORIGINAL matrix A. Row operations keep the dependence relations among the columns, but they change the column space itself.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 2, 0), (2, 4, 1), (3, 6, 1). Which set is a basis for Col A?
questions.explain: R₂ − 2R₁, R₃ − 3R₁, then R₃ − R₂ give the echelon form with rows (1, 2, 0), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0). The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so take columns 1 and 3 of the original A: (1, 2, 3) and (0, 1, 1). {(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)} are echelon-form columns. They span the plane z = 0, which does not contain (1, 2, 3). Column 2 is 2·(column 1), so any set containing both is dependent.

questions.q: Let A have rows (1, 2, 0), (2, 4, 1), (3, 6, 1). Which set is a basis for Nul A?
questions.explain: The reduced echelon form has rows (1, 2, 0), (0, 0, 1), (0, 0, 0). So x₁ = −2x₂ and x₃ = 0, with x₂ free, and x = x₂(−2, 1, 0). Check: each row of A dotted with (−2, 1, 0) gives 0. Count check: 2 pivots + 1 free variable = 3 columns.

questions.q: Let A = [v₁ v₂ v₃] with v₁ = (1, 1, −2), v₂ = (1, −1, 2), v₃ = (2, 0, 0). Its reduced echelon form has rows (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 0). Which set is a basis for Nul A?
questions.explain: x₁ = −x₃ and x₂ = −x₃, with x₃ free, so x = x₃(−1, −1, 1). This null vector is the dependence relation −v₁ − v₂ + v₃ = 0. (1, 1, 1) gives v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = (4, 0, 0), and (1, −1, 0) gives v₁ − v₂ = (0, 2, −4), so neither is in Nul A. There is a free variable, so the basis is not empty.

questions.q: The equation Ax = b is consistent exactly when b is in Col A.
questions.explain: Ax is a linear combination of the columns of A with weights from x. So Ax = b has a solution exactly when b is a combination of the columns, which means b is in Col A. This is why row reducing [A | b] with a symbolic b describes a span.
